name: Lake Tana Island Monasteries & Zege Peninsula
summary: A group of medieval Ethiopian Orthodox monasteries on the islands and Zege Peninsula of Lake Tana, known for painted round churches, church museums and coffee forest. Most visits are boat trips from Bahir Dar.
details:
Lake Tana, Ethiopia's largest lake, has dozens of churches and monasteries on its shores and islands. The Zege Peninsula on the southern shore is the most visited area. It is covered in dense coffee forest, which survives partly because of a long-standing religious ban on cutting trees and ploughing there.

Ura Kidane Mehret is the best-known church on Zege. The convent dates from the 14th century and its round church from the 16th century. It is known for its wall paintings and has a small museum of church treasures. Both men and women may enter. Other Zege churches include Azuwa Maryam (a round, thatched church), Bete Maryam, Bete Selassie and Tekla Haimanot; the last two are about a 45-minute uphill walk from the shore and Bete Selassie is men-only. Mehal Zege Giyorgis is described as the oldest, founded in 1264.

Further out, Dega Estefanos sits on a hill about 100 m above the lake and holds a 16th-century painting of the Madonna and the remains of several emperors. Narga Selassie, on Dek Island (the lake's largest), dates from the late 18th century. Tana Qirqos is a small island about three hours by boat from Bahir Dar, where tradition says the Ark of the Covenant was kept for centuries. Kebran Gabriel, closest to Bahir Dar, is no longer open to the public.

Several island monasteries do not admit women. Check which sites you plan to visit before you go.
highlights: Ura Kidane Mehret round church and its painted walls
Church museums with old manuscripts and crosses
Coffee forest walks on the Zege Peninsula
Longer boat trips to Dega Estefanos, Narga Selassie or Tana Qirqos
bestTimeToVisit: The dry season, roughly October to May, is generally easiest for boat trips and forest walks; the June–September rains can make the lake rougher and paths muddy.
gettingThere: Boats leave from the Bahir Dar port area; the crossing to the Zege Peninsula takes about 30–60 minutes depending on the boat. The peninsula can also be reached by land (sources give road distances of roughly 20–32 km). Island monasteries such as Tana Qirqos need half-day or longer boat trips.
tips: Women should check entry rules: some monasteries (for example Bete Selassie and several island sites) admit men only; Ura Kidane Mehret admits everyone.
Church museums usually charge a separate fee; one recent traveller report put Ura Kidane Mehret museum at about 250 birr, but confirm locally.
Remove shoes before entering churches and ask before photographing priests.
Agree the boat route, number of stops and price before leaving the port.

name: Debre Berhan Selassie Church, Gondar
summary: Gondar's most famous church, known for its ceiling painted with rows of winged angel faces and walls covered in biblical scenes. It is usually visited together with the Fasil Ghebbi castles.
details:
Debre Berhan Selassie ("Trinity and the Mountain of Light") is a walled church compound on the edge of Gondar. The original church dates from the late 17th century, built by one of the Gondarine emperors (sources differ on which Iyasu). Later sources say the church was rebuilt in the 1880s after damage from a Sudanese Dervish raid and a lightning strike.

The interior is the reason to visit. The ceiling is covered in rows of painted cherub faces with wings; one guide counts 135 around the upper walls and ceiling area, others give about 80 on the ceiling itself. The walls are painted from floor to roof with biblical scenes, saints and a vivid depiction of hell, used historically to teach people who could not read. The paintings are often attributed to the artist Haile Meskel.

The compound wall has twelve round towers said to represent the apostles and a larger thirteenth tower for the Lion of Judah. The conservation body ICCROM carried out restoration campaigns on the wall paintings between 1979 and 1982.

It is an active church; services are still held and priests usually guide visitors.
highlights: Painted ceiling of winged angel faces
Walled compound with twelve towers plus the Lion of Judah tower
Easy to combine with Fasil Ghebbi and Fasilides' Bath
bestTimeToVisit: Open all year. A 2020s operator page lists hours as 8:00–12:30 and 13:30–18:00. The dry season (October–May) is most comfortable; Timkat in January is busy in Gondar.
gettingThere: The church is on the northern edge of Gondar, within walking or short taxi distance of the town centre. Gondar has an airport with domestic flights from Addis Ababa and is roughly 180 km by road north of Bahir Dar.
tips: Remove shoes before entering.
By custom men use the main door and women the side door.
Tickets are paid in cash opposite the entrance; there is an extra charge for photography inside. One operator listed 50 birr entry and 75 birr for photos, but fees change.
A small tip for the priest who shows you around is customary.

name: Mekele (Mekelle)
summary: The capital of Tigray and a former imperial capital under Emperor Yohannes IV, used by travellers as a base for the Gheralta rock churches and the Danakil Depression.
details:
Mekele sits at about 2,250 m in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, roughly 780 km north of Addis Ababa. It grew from a small settlement into a town in the early 19th century, and in the 1880s Emperor Yohannes IV made it his political capital.

The historic centre is the Emperor Yohannes IV palace, built in 1882–84, which now houses a museum with the emperor's throne, royal bed and other items. Other landmarks include the 51 m Tigray Martyrs Memorial Monument in Adi-Haki, the large Monday market (Edaga Senuy) founded by Yohannes IV, and the Abreha Castle, a former palace now used as a hotel.

The city has been at the centre of the conflicts in Tigray since 2020. It was attacked in 2020, retaken by Tigrayan forces in 2021, and saw political upheaval in 2025. Wikipedia reports further military changes in October 2026.

Before the conflicts, Mekele was the usual starting point for tours to the Gheralta churches, Wukro, Negash and the Danakil Depression.
highlights: Emperor Yohannes IV Palace and Museum
bestTimeToVisit: The dry season, roughly October to March, is usual for northern highland travel. Under current advisories, travel is not recommended at all (see confidence notes).
gettingThere: Alula Aba Nega International Airport (MQX) has had domestic flights from Addis Ababa when services are running. By road Mekele is about 780 km north of Addis Ababa. Flights and roads into Tigray have been suspended at times during the conflicts; check current status.
tips: Confirm whether flights and roads into Tigray are operating before making any plans.
Carry ID and expect checkpoints.
Banking and communications in Tigray have been disrupted at times; do not rely on cards or mobile data.

name: Wukro Chirkos Rock-Hewn Church
summary: One of the most accessible rock-hewn churches in Tigray, carved from a sandstone outcrop on the northern edge of Wukro beside the main highway.
details:
Wukro Chirkos (Cherkos) is a monolithic church cut out of the rock on the edge of Wukro town, north of Mekele. It is dedicated to the child martyr Cyricus (Qirqos). Unlike many Tigray churches that require steep climbs, it can be reached easily from the main road.

Scholars date it to roughly AD 700–1000; local tradition links it to the brother kings Abreha and Atsbeha. It has a cross-in-square plan with a barrel-vaulted interior leading to the sanctuary, an Aksumite-style frieze above the columns, and an entrance porch with a central pillar.

The walls and ceilings show fire damage, which local tradition blames on the 16th-century campaigns of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi. A cement floor and a raised porch roof were added around 1958, and the compound now has a modern bell tower and gatehouse.

Wukro is a common stop between Mekele and the Gheralta churches or Adigrat, and Negash (with its historic mosque) is about 10 km further north.
highlights: Combine with Negash mosque 10 km north
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season, roughly October to March, has been usual. Under current advisories, travel is not recommended.
gettingThere: Wukro lies on the Mekele–Adigrat highway; Negash is about 10 km north of Wukro. Mekele is the nearest airport (when flights operate); the drive from Mekele is short, roughly under an hour (approximate).
tips: Remove shoes; a priest usually opens the church for visitors and a small donation is expected.
Mekele is the usual overnight base.

name: Negash and the Al-Nejashi Mosque
summary: A village on the Mekele–Adigrat road regarded as the earliest Muslim settlement in Africa, with one of the continent's oldest mosques and the tomb associated with the Aksumite king (Najashi) who sheltered early Muslims.
details:
Negash lies about 10 km north of Wukro on the Adigrat–Mekele road. It is considered the earliest Muslim settlement in Africa and is linked to the first migration (Hijra) of the Prophet Muhammad's followers to the Aksumite kingdom, whose king — known in Arabic as al-Najashi — gave them refuge.

The Al-Nejashi Mosque and the tomb complex, including tombs attributed to companions of the Prophet, make it an important pilgrimage site for Ethiopian Muslims. A 16th-century chronicle records that Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi visited the tomb of Ashama ibn Abjar here around 1537.

The mosque was restored by the Turkish agency TIKA in the 2010s. It was heavily damaged by shelling and looting during the 2020–2022 Tigray war. TIKA carried out new repairs from October 2024, completed in July 2025, covering the mausoleum dome, the minaret, walls and a hall.
highlights: One of the oldest mosques in Africa
Tomb complex linked to the first Hijra
Easy stop with Wukro Chirkos church
bestTimeToVisit: Dry season, roughly October to March, has been usual. Under current advisories, travel is not recommended.
gettingThere: On the main Mekele–Adigrat road, about 10 km north of Wukro. Mekele is the nearest airport when flights are operating.
tips: Dress modestly; women should cover hair and everyone should remove shoes in the mosque.
Ask before taking photographs, particularly during prayers.

name: Lake Afrera (Afdera)
summary: A hypersaline lake about 112 m below sea level in the Danakil Depression, where visitors float in salty water, soak in shoreline hot springs and see salt being produced.
details:
Lake Afrera, also spelled Afdera and once called Lake Giulietti, lies in Kilbet Rasu zone of the Afar Region at about 112 m below sea level. It covers about 115 km² and reaches about 80 m deep.

The lake is fed by many hot springs along its shore. Its salt comes from hydrothermal reactions with buried salt deposits and basalt, not from the sea, and its water is unusually acidic for an Ethiopian salt lake.

Salt has been collected here for centuries, and brine is pumped into evaporation ponds along the shore. Ash and gas from the 2011 Nabro eruption in Eritrea contaminated the lake and made the salt unfit to eat for a time.

For travellers, Afrera is usually a stop on multi-day Danakil Depression tours on the way to or from Erta Ale. The water is salty enough to float in easily, and a hot spring next to the lake is used as a natural bath. Tour groups often camp nearby.
highlights: Stark desert scenery below sea level
bestTimeToVisit: The cooler months, roughly November to February; summer temperatures in the Danakil are extremely high.
gettingThere: Usually visited on organised 3–4 day Danakil tours from Mekele or Semera. A traveller report describes the road from Semera toward Afrera as good tarmac, worsening after the turn-off into the Danakil. Permits and local Afar guides or escorts are typically arranged by the tour operator.
tips: Do not shave or swim with open cuts; the salt stings badly.
Bring quick-dry clothes and a spare towel; there are few rinsing facilities.
Carry plenty of drinking water and sun protection.
Go with an established operator; independent travel here needs permits and escorts.
confidenceNotes: Coordinates converted from Wikipedia's 13°17′N 40°55′E. Practical details come from tour operator pages. Camping is the norm; no hotels confirmed at the lake. The lake is in north-east Afar near the Eritrea border, so parts of the approach may fall in FCDO "advise against all travel" zones; check the FCDO map. name: Lake Abbe
summary: A remote salt lake on the Ethiopia–Djibouti border, famous for its fields of steaming limestone chimneys up to 50 m tall and its flamingos.
details:
Lake Abbe is a salt lake on the border between Ethiopia and Djibouti, at the Afar triple junction where three tectonic plates meet. It is the final destination of the Awash River and the last of a chain of connected lakes.

The lake is best known for its carbonate (limestone) chimneys, some up to about 50 m tall, which vent steam. They formed where lake water mixed with hot geothermal fluid rising from below. Flamingos feed on the lake.

The lake has shrunk a great deal since the 1940s, mainly because water is taken from the Awash upstream. Its surface lies at about 243 m above sea level.

The area is described as one of the most inaccessible places on earth. Lonely Planet notes that from the Ethiopian side it is at least a three-day trip, and that it is much easier to reach from Djibouti, where most tourist visits to the chimneys start.
bestTimeToVisit: The cooler months, roughly November to February; temperatures are extreme in summer.
gettingThere: From Ethiopia, access is via Semera and Asaita with permits from the Semera tourist office; the trip is at least three days and may require an armed escort. Most visitors reach the lake from the Djibouti side instead.
tips: Arrange permits in Semera and travel with an experienced operator and local Afar guide.
Carry fuel, water and food; there are no services near the lake.
Consider visiting from Djibouti, which is easier.
confidenceNotes: Very little current, first-hand travel information from the Ethiopian side. Wikipedia gives inconsistent area figures. Escort requirement comes from a Lonely Planet listing and may have changed. name: Asaita (Aussa)
summary: A historic Afar town on the Awash River, once capital of the Adal Sultanate and the Sultanate of Aussa, and the gateway to the salt lakes near the Djibouti border.
details:
Asaita, historically called Aussa, lies at about 300 m above sea level in the Awash valley in central Afar. It was the capital of the Afar Region until 2007, when the newly built town of Semera took over.

The town has a long history. Farming here dates to at least the 14th century. It briefly became the capital of the Adal Sultanate in 1577, then the seat of the Imamate of Aussa, and from the 18th century the Sultanate of Aussa, the main Afar monarchy, ruled from here.

About 20 salt lakes lie south-east of Asaita toward the Djibouti border. Lake Gummare (Gamari) is known for flamingos and Lake Abbe, with its limestone chimneys, is the end point of the Awash River.

Asaita is mainly of interest as a base for these lakes and as a glimpse of Afar town life.
highlights: Historic seat of the Sultanate of Aussa
Gateway to Lakes Afambo, Gummare and Abbe
bestTimeToVisit: November to February, when temperatures are lower.
gettingThere: Asaita is about 50 km south of the Awash–Assab highway. A paved road links it with Semera, the regional capital, which has an airport. Permits for the nearby lakes are obtained from the Semera tourist office.
tips: Get permission papers at the Semera tourist office before heading to the lakes.
Expect very high temperatures; travel early in the day.
Dress conservatively; Afar communities are Muslim.

name: Babile Elephant Sanctuary
summary: A large protected area south of Harar that shelters one of Ethiopia's last elephant populations, along with dry acacia woodland, rocky valleys and many birds.
details:
The Babile Elephant Sanctuary covers about 6,982 km² in Babile district, East Hararghe Zone, in eastern Ethiopia, about 40 km south of Harar. It was set up around 1970 to protect a remnant population of north-east African elephants and takes in the valleys of the Erer, Dakata, Fafen, Gobele and Borale rivers.

At least 200–300 elephants have been recorded, and a 2004–2008 study estimated the sanctuary holds about 27% of Ethiopia's elephants. They live mainly in the western part of the reserve.

Other wildlife includes hamadryas baboon, Günther's dik-dik, greater and lesser kudu, Soemmerring's gazelle and Menelik's bushbuck, with lion, leopard and hyenas also recorded. About 227 bird species have been noted, including Salvadori's seedeater, which is endemic to this part of Ethiopia.

The sanctuary faces serious threats from poaching, farming, overgrazing and invasive plants, and much of the north-west has been converted to farmland. Seeing elephants is not guaranteed and usually needs a guide and an early start.
highlights: One of Ethiopia's remaining elephant populations
Dry acacia woodland and river valleys
Can be combined with the Dakata Valley of Marvels and Harar
bestTimeToVisit: The drier months, roughly October to March, make tracks easier to drive; elephant sightings depend on local conditions at any time.
gettingThere: The sanctuary lies about 40 km south of Harar and about 560 km east of Addis Ababa. Most visitors base themselves in Harar (reached by road or by flying to Dire Dawa) and arrange a 4x4 and local guide.
tips: Hire a local guide or scout; elephants range widely and tracks are rough.
A 4x4 vehicle is needed for the interior.
Treat elephants with caution; human–elephant conflict is common here.
confidenceNotes: Region is Oromia (East Hararghe), not Somali; the sanctuary borders Somali region. Coordinates converted from Wikipedia's 8°45′N 42°38′E. Elephant numbers are from older studies and may be lower now. Visitor facilities and fees not confirmed; no lodges confirmed inside the sanctuary (Harar hotels are the usual base). name: Dakata Valley (Valley of Marvels)
summary: A valley of wind-carved rock towers and balancing boulders near Babile, on the road between Harar and Jijiga.
details:
The Dakata (Dakhata) Valley, often called the Valley of Marvels, is an area of tall rock towers, pillars and balanced boulders shaped by wind and water. Travel writers compare the scenery to parts of Utah.

The most striking stretch starts about 4 km east of Babile on the road from Harar to Jijiga. Some formations are visible from the road, but Lonely Planet recommends a half-day walk with a guide to see the area properly.

The valley lies within the Babile Elephant Sanctuary, which takes in the valleys of the Erer, Dakata and Fafen rivers.

Babile town is also known for its camel market, and the valley is an easy stop for anyone travelling between Harar and Jijiga.
highlights: Easy stop on the Harar–Jijiga road
bestTimeToVisit: Early morning or late afternoon for cooler walking and better light; the drier months (roughly October–March) are easiest.
gettingThere: Babile is on the Harar–Jijiga road, a little over 30 km east of Harar (approximate). The valley begins about 4 km east of Babile.
tips: Take a local guide for walks off the road.
Bring water and sun protection.
Combine with Harar or a trip on to Jijiga.

name: Jijiga (Jigjiga)
summary: The capital of Ethiopia's Somali Region, a fast-growing trading city near the Somaliland border with Somali culture, markets and nearby historic sites.
details:
Jijiga sits at about 1,640 m in eastern Ethiopia and is the largest city and capital of the Somali Region, which moved its capital here from Gode in 1995.

The town grew around an imperial garrison set up in 1891. It was attacked by Dervish forces in 1900, occupied by Italy in 1936 and by British forces in 1941, and returned to Ethiopian administration in 1948.

Places of interest mentioned in sources include a cave associated with the local leader Garad Wiil Waal (after whom the airport is named), a mosque said to date to 1315 from the Harla period, the scenic Hamran mountain in Awbare district, and a Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan statue.

For most visitors Jijiga is a stop on the way to the Somaliland border at Wajale (Togochale) or a destination for experiencing Somali culture, markets and food.
highlights: Gateway to the Wajale border crossing
bestTimeToVisit: October to March is generally drier and cooler, though the climate is warm year-round.
gettingThere: Garad Wiil-Waal Jijiga Airport has domestic flights. By road Jijiga is east of Harar via Babile and the Dakata valley; the main road continues to Wajale on the Somaliland border.
tips: Dress conservatively; the region is predominantly Muslim.
Stay on main routes; FCDO restrictions apply to areas closer to the Somalia border.
Ask before photographing people.

name: Lake Hayk and Hayk Istifanos Monastery
summary: A freshwater highland lake north of Dessie with a 13th-century monastery on a wooded peninsula, good birdwatching and lakeside walks.
details:
Lake Hayk lies at about 2,030 m in South Wollo, north of Dessie. It covers about 23 km² and is up to 88 m deep. The town of Hayk is on its western side.

Hayk Istifanos (Estifanos) Monastery stands on a wooded peninsula, formerly an island, on the lake's western shore. It was founded in the mid-13th century by Iyasus Mo'a, a teacher of Tekle Haymanot. Iyasus Mo'a helped Yekuno Amlak restore the Solomonic dynasty, and the church became an important monastery when Yekuno Amlak took the throne. The monastery has a museum of old manuscripts and treasures.

Women are not permitted to enter the monastery but may visit the adjacent nunnery.

The lake is one of the better birding spots in the region. The Portuguese priest Francisco Álvares, the first known European to see it, passed by in 1520.
highlights: Easy side trip from Dessie or Kombolcha
bestTimeToVisit: October to May is generally drier; one guide suggests late spring through September. Birdlife is varied year-round.
gettingThere: Hayk town is about 20–30 km north of Dessie (sources differ). Dessie is about 400 km north of Addis Ababa by road, and Kombolcha airport serves both towns. The monastery can be reached on foot from Hayk town.
tips: Women cannot enter the monastery itself but can visit the nunnery.
Dessie and Kombolcha are the usual overnight bases.
Bring binoculars for birdwatching.

name: Dessie and Kombolcha
summary: Twin towns in the South Wollo highlands that serve as a stopover between Addis Ababa and Lalibela, with a museum, a historic palace and nearby Lake Hayk.
details:
Dessie sits at about 2,470 m in the South Wollo Zone, about 400 km north of Addis Ababa. Emperor Yohannes IV founded it in 1882 and named it "My Joy" after a comet he saw there. It later became the base of Ras Mikael and the capital of Wollo Province until 1995.

Sights include a museum in the former home of Dejazmach Yoseph Birru, the palace of Ras (Negus) Mikael and the church of Enda Medhane Alem. Dessie is also an important Islamic centre, with an early zawiya of the Qadiriyya Sufi order.

Kombolcha, a lower industrial town nearby, shares Combolcha Airport (DSE) with Dessie.

The towns were occupied by TPLF-aligned forces in late 2021 and retaken by the government in December 2021. Most travellers use them as an overnight stop or a base for Lake Hayk.
bestTimeToVisit: October to May is generally drier.
gettingThere: About 400 km north of Addis Ababa by road. Combolcha Airport (DSE) near Kombolcha serves both towns when domestic flights operate.

name: Guassa Community Conservation Area (Menz)
summary: A high Afroalpine plateau managed by local communities for over 400 years, and one of the best places to see Ethiopian wolves and geladas outside the national parks.
details:
The Guassa Community Conservation Area covers about 100 km² of Afroalpine grassland at 3,200–3,700 m in Menz-Gera district, North Shewa Zone. The district capital, Mehal Meda, is about 20 km away.

The area has been managed for more than 400 years under a local system called Qero, in which elected leaders control grazing and grass cutting. The Guassa grass that gives the area its name is used for thatch and rope. The system collapsed after the 1974 land reform and was later revived with conservation support.

Nine endemic mammals live here, including the Ethiopian wolf (with about six packs), the gelada and the Ethiopian highland hare. About 114 bird species have been recorded, including the Ankober serin, Abyssinian catbird, blue-winged goose and wattled ibis. Giant lobelias and Erica moorland add to the scenery.

Community-led trekking, from day walks to three-night routes, has been supported by the Frankfurt Zoological Society. The community lodge reopened after closures during COVID-19 and the war, and a new lodge was reported to be under construction.
bestTimeToVisit: The dry season, roughly October to February, gives clearer skies and easier walking; nights are cold all year at this altitude.
gettingThere: Reached by road from Addis Ababa via Debre Birhan; the area is about 80 km off the main highway, with Mehal Meda about 20 km away. Tour operators run trips of one or more days; a 4x4 is advisable.
tips: Pack warm clothing; temperatures can drop below freezing at night.
Book the community lodge or camping through a tour operator or the community in advance.
Hire community guides; fees support local conservation.

name: Ankober
summary: A former royal capital of the Shewa kingdom on the edge of the eastern escarpment, with palace ruins, old churches, sweeping views and the endemic Ankober serin.
details:
Ankober sits at about 2,465 m on the eastern escarpment of the Ethiopian Highlands, about 40 km east of Debre Birhan and about 140 km north-east of Addis Ababa.

It was the main royal seat of the Shewa kingdom from the early 19th century until Menelik II moved his capital to Entoto in 1878. Menelik later used the town to hold political prisoners. While he was away at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, the town was pillaged.

On the palace hill, a long stone-and-mortar wall survives from Menelik's palace, and the Kidus Mikael church was built by Sahle Selassie. Ankober Palace Lodge, a lodge built in traditional style on the old palace grounds, offers guided walks around the hill and its churches.

The area is also known to birdwatchers as the type locality of the Ankober serin, an endemic finch first recorded in 1979, which lives on the escarpment cliffs.
highlights: Menelik II palace hill and remains
Escarpment views over the Rift lowlands
Ankober serin and other highland birds
bestTimeToVisit: October to May is generally drier; the escarpment can be misty in the rainy season.
gettingThere: About 40 km east of Debre Birhan; tour itineraries put the drive from Addis Ababa at about 3–4 hours (roughly 150 km).
tips: Bring warm clothes; it is cool and windy on the palace hill.
Ask the lodge about guided tours of the palace hill and church opening times.
Birders should look for the Ankober serin on the escarpment cliffs.
